title: How I check AI-assisted movie puzzles: verify all 36 matches, then the whole lineup
author: Parking-Cash3586
selftext:
I make Cast Six with AI coding assistance, including OpenAI Codex. It's a browser game with six movies and six overlapping clues. A film can fit more than one clue, but there must be one complete lineup using every film once.



The useful development lesson is that 'the solver found one answer' isn't enough. A unique answer can still be based on a false movie fact.



Our collection-validation code checks the 36 film/clue pairs against the catalog and recorded evidence, then checks that the solver returns exactly the intended solution. Cast, director and release-decade matches are checked from structured data. Editorial clues need their own definitions and evidence.



For an easier collection, there is another check I like: examine the arrangements with five correct matches and count how many movies would have to move to finish. A board can have familiar films and still feel unfair if almost the entire lineup has to move after a near-solve. With six films there are only 720 permutations, so exhaustive checks are practical.



Those checks do not prove the catalog is accurate or that a clue feels fair to a person. Source review and playtesting still matter. AI review also shouldn't be described as independent human review.



If you want to see the mechanic: [https://www.castsix.com/?utm\_source=reddit&utm\_medium=community&utm\_campaign=october\_outreach&utm\_content=aigamedev](https://www.castsix.com/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=community&utm_campaign=october_outreach&utm_content=aigamedev)



The daily and archive are free without an account or download. Movie facts and posters come from TMDB. For anyone building a puzzle with AI assistance: what do you validate separately from the solver?
